name: Reflection
kicker: Waves bouncing off a surface · How mirrors and echoes work
dates: Law known since ancient Greek times
briefing: Reflection is what happens when a wave bounces off a surface instead of passing through it. A smooth mirror sends light away at the same angle it arrived, which keeps the image sharp, and sound bouncing off a canyon wall comes back as an echo. Even moonlight is just sunlight bouncing off the Moon’s surface.
answerHtml: reflection (accept word forms like reflecting; accept specific types such as specular reflection, diffuse reflection, or total internal reflection; do not accept “refraction” or “diffraction”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Apollo astronauts left panels of corner-cube prisms on the Moon that send laser light straight back toward Earth, letting scientists measure that the Moon drifts about 3.8 centimeters farther away each year. Bicycle and road-sign safety markers work the same way.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this bouncing of a wave off a surface, which lets you see yourself in a mirror.

tossups.p: Hero of Alexandria showed that light traveling from an object to a flat, polished surface and then to an eye takes the shortest possible route, an early version of Fermat’s principle. The incoming ray, the outgoing ray, and the line perpendicular to the surface, called the normal, all lie in one plane.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this effect described by a law stating that light leaves a mirror at the same angle at which it arrived.

tossups.p: At Brewster’s angle, light bouncing off a sheet of glass becomes completely polarized, and the bounced ray and the bent ray travel at right angles to each other. Polarized sunglasses cut glare because light bouncing off a flat road or lake is partly polarized.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this bouncing of light off a surface, which makes the image you see in a mirror.

tossups.p: The Fresnel [“fray-NEL”] equations give the fraction of light sent back at a boundary between two materials; for light hitting ordinary glass straight on, that fraction is only about 4 percent. That is why you can faintly see yourself in a shop window.
tossups.r: A flat mirror uses this effect to make an upright image that seems to sit behind the glass. For 10 points, name this bouncing of a wave off a surface.

tossups.p: Coatings on eyeglasses and camera lenses are made about a quarter of a wavelength thick, so the light waves bouncing back from the top and bottom of each coating cancel out and glare is reduced. Stealth aircraft are shaped to send radar waves away from the receiver instead of back toward it.
tossups.r: Smooth surfaces make a sharp “specular” kind of this effect. For 10 points, name this bouncing of light, which lets a mirror form an image.

tossups.p: A pulse sent along a rope tied to a wall comes back upside down, while a pulse on a rope with a loose end comes back right side up. Light picks up a similar half-wavelength flip when it bounces off a material in which it travels more slowly.
tossups.r: Echoes are an example of this effect. For 10 points, name this bouncing of waves off a surface.

tossups.p: Past the critical angle, light inside glass cannot escape through the surface and all of it bounces back inside, which lets optical fibers carry signals over long distances. The same trick makes a cut diamond sparkle and lets prisms fold the light path inside binoculars.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this bouncing of light off a surface, which is how a mirror works.

tossups.p: A layer behind the retina called the tapetum lucidum [“tuh-PEE-tum LOO-sih-dum”] makes the eyes of cats and deer glow in headlights by sending light back through the eye. Road markers called “cat’s eyes” use glass beads or prisms to send headlight beams back toward drivers.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this effect, in which a wave bounces off a surface, as light does from a mirror.

tossups.p: In 1668, Isaac Newton built a telescope that gathered light with a curved metal dish instead of a glass lens, which avoided the colored fringes that lenses create. Most large modern telescopes also collect light with curved surfaces instead of lenses, and the James Webb Space Telescope’s curved surfaces are coated with gold.
tossups.r: Those telescopes depend on this effect. For 10 points, name this bouncing of light off a surface, which lets a mirror form an image.

tossups.p: David Brewster patented the kaleidoscope in 1817; its endlessly repeating patterns come from light bouncing back and forth between two or three long, shiny strips set at an angle. Submarine crews use periscopes, which bounce light off two surfaces tilted at 45 degrees, to look above the water.
tossups.r: Both devices rely on mirrors. For 10 points, name this effect in which light bounces off a surface.

tossups.p: A surface’s albedo is the fraction of sunlight it sends back; fresh snow has a very high albedo, and dark ocean water has a low one. Saturn’s icy moon Enceladus [“en-SEL-uh-dus”] sends back most of the sunlight that hits it.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this bouncing of light off a surface, which lets you see yourself in a mirror.

tossups.p: Leonardo da Vinci correctly explained the faint glow on the dark part of a crescent Moon, called earthshine, as sunlight bounced off Earth and then off the Moon. Ordinary moonlight is also just sunlight sent back by the Moon’s surface.
tossups.r: Because of this effect, drivers can read the backward word “AMBULANCE” on an ambulance’s front in their rearview mirrors. For 10 points, name this bouncing of light off a surface.

tossups.p: Legends claim that Archimedes used polished bronze shields to focus sunlight and set Roman ships on fire during the siege of Syracuse. Solar power towers use fields of shiny panels to aim sunlight at one spot in the same way.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this effect in which light bounces off a shiny surface, such as a mirror.

tossups.p: A car headlight puts its bulb at the focus of a curved, bowl-shaped surface, so the light leaves in a parallel beam; a satellite dish works the same way in reverse. For a spherical curve, that focus lies halfway between the surface and its center of curvature.
tossups.r: Concave and convex mirrors both rely on this effect. For 10 points, name this bouncing of light off a surface.

tossups.p: In the Whispering Gallery of St. Paul’s Cathedral in London, a whisper near the curved wall can be heard far across the dome because the sound keeps bouncing along the wall. Bats and dolphins find food by listening for sounds that come back to them.
tossups.r: Those returning sounds are echoes. For 10 points, name this bouncing of a wave off a surface.

trap.title: Bounce, bend, or spread?
trap.body: Reflection, refraction, and diffraction sound alike and all describe a wave meeting something, so real tossups are strict about which one they want. Reflection is a wave bouncing back off a surface and staying in the same material. Refraction is bending as the wave crosses into a new material and changes speed, and diffraction is spreading around an edge or through a narrow opening.
trap.fix: Mirrors, echoes, equal angles, albedo, or light sent back the way it came mean reflection. A bent straw, lenses, Snell’s law, or a prism means refraction; slits, gratings, Bragg’s law, or sound bending around corners means diffraction.
trap.line: Real answer line: reflection (accept word forms like reflecting; accept specific types such as specular reflection, diffuse reflection, or total internal reflection; do not accept “refraction” or “diffraction”)
